opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few directions that matter a lot, and they're connected.

The first is moving from benchmarks to real utility. For a long time the field has been about training a better model and then measuring it on some exam-like benchmark. Those benchmarks are mostly self-contained: you get a question, you produce an answer, and you're scored independently each time. Real work isn't like that. The more important question now is how we define tasks and evaluations that reflect what people actually need, where an agent works over a long horizon, interacts with humans, and gets judged on whether it really created value. I sometimes describe this as the "second half" of AI. The first half was about methods. The second half is about defining the right problems and the right evaluations.

The second is memory and long-term context. Today most agents are still kind of stateless. Each task starts from scratch. A human employee gets better over months at the same job because they accumulate context about the company, the people, and what worked or failed before. If agents can't do that, there's a ceiling on how useful they can be, no matter how smart the base model is. So I think long-term memory, and more generally learning while deployed, is going to be very important.

The third is about the environment and the interface. A lot of agent capability is limited not by the model but by what the agent can access and how it acts. Is it working through a browser, through code, through APIs, through a computer? Designing good action spaces and good environments is underrated. Coding agents have progressed quickly partly because the environment is so clean: there's a terminal, there are tests, there's feedback.

Related to that is reward and feedback. In math or coding you have a verifiable signal. For most real tasks, like writing a good report, negotiating, doing research, the reward is fuzzy or delayed. How agents learn from human feedback, from their own reflection, or from some kind of intrinsic motivation in those settings is an open problem. I think it's one of the deepest ones.

Finally, there's the product side, which I think researchers sometimes underestimate. The interaction paradigm isn't settled yet. Chat was the first form factor, but it may not be the right one for agents that run for hours or days. Questions like when the agent should ask the human something, how much autonomy to give it, and how people supervise it are partly research questions and partly product design questions. The companies and teams that figure out that combination, model plus environment plus interaction, will probably define the next phase.

So if I had to summarize: less focus on making the model score higher on a fixed exam, and more on long-horizon tasks, memory, feedback in messy real-world settings, and finding the right way for humans and agents to work together.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the bottleneck has shifted. For a long time the question was whether the model could reason well enough, and I spent a lot of my PhD on that side, with things like ReAct and Tree of Thoughts, trying to get language models to actually think and act in a loop. But now the models are quite capable, and if you look at where agents actually fail in practice, it's much less about the model's raw intelligence and much more about three things: the environment, the evaluation, and the ability to learn from experience.

Let me take those one at a time.

First, environments. I like to say that the second half of AI is less about new training methods and more about defining the right problems. An agent is only as interesting as the world it lives in. Right now most agents operate in environments that are either very narrow, like a single coding repo or a browser with a fixed set of sites, or very artificial, like text games. What we need are environments that are rich, open-ended, and grounded in real utility, where the agent can take many actions, get real feedback, and where success actually matters to someone. That's partly why I think of things like SWE-bench or tau-bench as more than just benchmarks. They're attempts to carve out a slice of the real world that an agent can be trained and measured in.

Second, evaluation. This sounds boring but I think it's actually the crux. Our evaluation setups are still mostly i.i.d., single-shot, and automated. But real agent work is sequential, long-horizon, interactive, and often involves a human who changes their mind halfway through. If you can't measure that, you can't optimize for it. So I'd put a lot of weight on building evaluations that look like real deployments: long tasks, partial credit, costs for taking too long or asking too many questions, and users who are simulated well enough to be adversarial. Whoever gets this right will quietly define what "good agent" means.

Third, and maybe the one I'm most excited about, is memory and continual learning. Today's agents mostly reset every episode. They don't accumulate experience across tasks the way a new employee does. The interesting direction is agents that can reflect on what happened, store what's useful, and get better the next time, without a full retraining cycle. Reflexion was a very primitive version of that idea, but I think the mature version involves tighter integration between the model's reasoning, its external memory, and some form of reinforcement learning over long horizons. That's where language agents stop being tools and start being something closer to collaborators.

If I had to compress all of that: build better worlds, measure what actually matters, and let the agent remember. The models will keep improving on their own. The rest is on us.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important shift is from building agents that can do something impressive once to building agents that can reliably finish useful work. Those are quite different goals. An agent might succeed on each individual step most of the time, but when a task requires many steps, small errors accumulate. So we need better ways for agents to check their progress, recognize mistakes, and recover.

One direction is learning through interaction. An agent takes an action, observes what happened, and decides what to do next. We want models to get better at that whole process, including knowing when to explore, when to verify an answer, and when to ask a person for clarification.

Another direction is evaluation. If we only measure whether an agent solves a short, clearly specified task, we miss a lot of what makes real work difficult. In practice, the goal can be ambiguous, the environment can change, and success may depend on information the agent has to discover. We need evaluations that capture those situations, along with the time and cost required to finish.

And I think there’s a lot of room in the interaction between models and the systems around them—tools, memory, and interfaces. A stronger model helps, but so does giving it the right information and a way to see whether its actions worked. The question I’d focus on is: can we give an agent a meaningful task, let it work with reasonable independence, and trust it to either finish or clearly explain where it needs help?

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important direction is moving from agents that can complete a short, well-defined task to agents that can work reliably over a much longer horizon. Taking an action is often relatively easy. The harder part is knowing whether that action helped, recognizing when something went wrong, and deciding how to recover. So planning, execution, and evaluation need to form a continuous loop.

Another direction is learning from experience. Today, a lot of agent development involves manually designing prompts and workflows. We need better ways for an agent to use feedback from its environment to improve—not just remember what happened, but change how it approaches the next problem.

And I think evaluation is central to both. If we only measure whether an agent succeeds on a short benchmark, we may miss whether it can handle ambiguity, ask a useful question, or recover from a mistake. We need tasks and environments that make those capabilities measurable.

Ultimately, I’m interested in the transition from producing a plausible answer to accomplishing something whose success we can actually verify.
